findings.summary: Build slots are held per cargo run, but lanes are described as owned by one job at a time. The two do not fit together.
findings.evidence: Section 4.2 has each cargo run take whichever slot lock it wins first, so its lane is 'lane k'. Section 4.3 releases the slot when cargo exits. Option A and step 5, however, say a lane is 'used by one job at a time and trimmed ... after each job'. With per-run slots, runs from different jobs interleave in a lane, and one job's runs land in different lanes. Then either the trim happens per run, which loses the producer's incremental workspace build between its own cargo calls and adds build seconds against the 135 s threshold in section 6.5, or lanes hold several jobs' workspace output, so the L estimate understates lane size. A simpler fix is to give each job a preferred lane (reacquire the last lane it used) or to hold the lane per job and only the CPU slot per run. Step 5's lane-size measurement would expose the problem, but the design should settle it.

summary: The change adds one file, docs/design/many-agents-few-builds.md, and does what the request asks. It splits wall time into model time, local check time and waiting across 59 jobs from 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-05. It lists every job in an appendix and names the record files and fields each figure comes from. I checked these against the evidence snapshot. Job 20261103-015346-82n3 matches exactly: wall 3842 s, model 2175 s (sum of 8 invocations) and local checks 970 s (baseline 1.9 + 38.4 + 929.8 s; verification checks reused from CI at 0 s). The job count of 59 matches: 64 outcome.json files, minus 5 jobs that have no invocations/ directory. The per-day counts (20 of 26 jobs had local check time; 974 s on 2026-11-05) and the 28 landed jobs also match. The note separates agent slots from build slots, defines a file-lock queue in arrival order, and says how a slot is taken and released for Athena's checks and for the agent's cargo. It compares five ways to share compiled output, recommends per-slot lanes plus smaller targets, and estimates about 0.9 GB per job against 10 to 12 GB. It works out 16 to 20 agents and 2 builds from 4 CPUs, 15 GB of memory and 27 GB of disk, and says MAX_CONCURRENCY_CEILING must rise from 8 to 32. It ends with 9 build steps, each naming its files and how its effect is measured. The code it names exists where it says, apart from one wrong path. Unmeasured figures are labelled as estimates. The findings are minor: a design gap where build slots are held per cargo run but lanes are owned per job, a wrong file location for remove_produce, and no CHANGELOG entry. The request's one-file limit takes precedence over the changelog default here.
